title: A Note on Leadership Style: Consistency Is Not Sameness
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership note argues that leaders who take the advice to be consistent too literally end up practicing sameness instead. The author separates what must stay fixed, namely values, standards, fairness and objectivity, from what must flex, namely goals, strategy and tactics. Citing leadership-effectiveness research and a recent meta-analysis, the piece claims that behavioral range and cognitive flexibility predict leader effectiveness better than uniformity does. It gives the example of a seasoned performer and an anxious newcomer needing different coaching, and a team on a settled process needing different support from a team in crisis. The newest research suggests the best teams help their leader sense when conditions have shifted. The closing guide question is: given what I stand for, what does this person, moment or situation need from me?
points: Consistency belongs to values and standards, while goals, strategy and tactics should adapt to the person and moment.
Sameness is a habit that answers only what the leader will do next, and it quietly signals inattention rather than discipline.
Behavioral range and cognitive flexibility are the strongest predictors of leader effectiveness in the research cited.
The best teams help their leader notice when conditions have changed and a different approach is needed.
quotes: Leaders are told, rightly so, that consistency builds trust and believability. Unfortunately, some leaders take this idea too literally.
Studies of leadership effectiveness repeatedly confirm that the best leaders are not the most uniform but the most versatile.
Values, standards, timeless behaviors, and universal qualities like fairness and objectivity must stay fixed. They don’t change from situation to situation or from person to person.
A seasoned performer and an anxious newcomer need different types of guidance and coaching.
Leaders who apply one method everywhere aren’t being consistent. They are being inattentive.
Good leaders are the same person every time. They do not do the same thing every time.
Sameness keeps a team where it is. Consistency takes it somewhere better.
